newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Israel upbeat, PLO glum after U.S.-brokered talks.
newsitem.headline: Israel upbeat, PLO glum after U.S.-brokered talks.

text.p: Israel was upbeat but the PLO on Thursday condemned as a failure a U.S. envoy's peace efforts that brought Israeli and Palestinian officials together for a high-level meeting on restarting formal talks.
"I believe that Dennis Ross's current mission has failed," senior Palestinian negotiator Saeb Erekat told Voice of Palestine radio, saying the envoy had focused only on procedural issues.

"The U.S. administration must commit Israel to what has been signed," he said, referring to peace deals which the PLO contends Israel violated by breaking ground in March for a Jewish settlement in annexed East Jerusalem.

Erekat, who holds the local government portfolio in the Palestinian cabinet, and Planning Minister Nabil Shaath on Wednesday met Israeli defence chief Yitzhak Mordechai and Yitzhak Molcho, an adviser to Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu.
From their leaders' differing assessments, it seemed as if each side had not been at the same three-hour session which Ross arranged at the residence of the U.S. ambassador to Israel.

"I think yesterday's meeting was a preliminary one which creates the basis for additional rounds of talks which we will have to agree upon," Netanyahu told members of his ruling coalition in Tel Aviv.
Netanyahu said the summer session of parliament, due to start next week, would be held "under the sign of a resumption of talks" broken off over the East Jerusalem settlement.

"In the end, the (formal) talks will be resumed because it is in the interest of both sides to resume them. As to their form...this will have to be discussed in deliberations which I believe will take a good number of days," he said.
A dour-looking Palestinian President Yasser Arafat took a different view.
"I am sorry to say very little progress had been achieved more than the meeting itself...nothing had been agreed," he told reporters in the West Bank town of Ramallah.
The PLO has demanded Israel halt settlement work before peace talks can resume.
Ross met Netanyahu on Thursday to brief him on the talks and planned to see the prime minister again later in the day before meeting Arafat and leaving for home on Friday.
Israeli Foreign Minister David Levy was due to meet U.S. Secretary of State Madeleine Albright in Washington on Friday on the Middle East peace crisis.

"It won't be solved in one conversation or in a day but it seems to me there is a beginning here, and with patience and by sticking to the positions upon which we must stand firm, we can perhaps achieve progress," Netanyahu said.

Israeli leaders have said they will not stop work at the East Jerusalem site they call Har Homa, insisting Jews have a right to live in all of the biblical Land of Israel, which includes the hill known to Palestinians as Jabal Abu Ghneim.

Speaking to the coalition members, Netanyahu also reiterated that a resumption of peace talks had to be in tandem with renewed security cooperation with the Palestinian Authority in the West Bank and Gaza.

Netanyahu was elected on a peace-with-security platform nearly a year ago and has increasingly pressed home the issue since a Tel Aviv cafe blast two months ago that killed a Palestinian bomber and three Israeli women.
The Israeli leader said he hoped the peace process would move in the direction of negotiations on a permanent peace accord with the PLO.

The PLO has already rejected Netanyahu's proposal to go straight into so-called final-status talks, which would tackle the highly sensitive issues of Jerusalem and Jewish settlements, rather than continue with interim peace moves.

Israel annexed East Jerusalem and declared all of the city its eternal and indivisible capital after the 1967 Middle East war. The PLO wants East Jerusalem as the capital of a future Palestinian state.
